about: The scripted AI lesson for p1-conservation (2026-11-17, Phase B, brief docs/briefs/2026-11-15-script-four-topics.md): every word she sees is written here once and checked (tools/check-script.js, tools/review-lesson.js --script). The AI only marks her typed answers (choosing a branch written here), answers her own questions, and sorts her messages. It opens with two recall questions from p1-energy-stores and p1-kinetic-potential.

keyPoints.heading: The law of conservation of energy

steps.text: Welcome! This lesson follows energy as it moves between stores and spreads out, and looks at the ways engineers reduce the energy that is wasted.

steps.question: First, two quick questions from earlier lessons. Which store does a hot cup of tea have a lot of energy in?
steps.right: Yes: hot things have a lot of energy in their thermal store.

wrong.other: Not quite: thermal. The thermal store depends on how hot something is.
wrong.kinetic: Not quite: thermal. The tea is not moving; it is hot, and the thermal store depends on how hot something is.
wrong.elastic: Not quite: thermal. Nothing is stretched; the tea is hot, and the thermal store depends on how hot something is.

idk.hint: The tea is hot. Which store depends on how hot something is?

steps.answerWhy: The thermal store depends on how hot something is.

steps.question: Second: a car brakes and slows down. Which store of the brakes gets more energy?
steps.right: Yes: rubbing makes the brakes hot, so their thermal store rises.

wrong.other: Not quite: their thermal store, because the brakes get hot.
wrong.kinetic: Not quite: the brakes get hot, so their thermal store gets more energy. It is the car's kinetic store that loses energy.
wrong.elastic: Not quite: nothing is stretched or squashed. The brakes get hot, so their thermal store rises.

idk.hint: Brakes get hot when they rub. Which store depends on how hot something is?

steps.answerWhy: Rubbing makes the brakes hot, so their thermal store rises.

steps.text: Now this lesson. Energy cannot be created or destroyed: it can only be moved from one store to another. That is the law of conservation of energy, and it holds for everything, every time.
Think of a ball bouncing. As it falls, energy moves from its gravitational potential store, the energy of being raised up, to its kinetic store, the energy of moving.
As the ball squashes against the floor, energy is briefly in its elastic potential store. As it springs back up, energy goes back through the kinetic store into the gravitational potential store.

steps.question: Each bounce is a little lower than the one before. Why?

options.text: Some energy goes to warming and sound
The ball's energy is slowly destroyed

steps.right: Yes. Each bounce makes a sound and warms the ball and floor very slightly, so less energy is left to lift the ball next time.

wrong.other: Not quite. On each bounce, some energy warms the ball and floor or leaves as sound, so less is left for the next one.
wrong.destroyed: Not quite: energy is never destroyed. On each bounce, some of it warms the ball and floor or leaves as sound, so less is left to lift the ball.
wrong.gravity: Not quite: gravity stays the same. On each bounce, some energy warms the ball and floor or leaves as sound, so less is left to lift the ball.

idk.hint: You hear each bounce, and the ball and floor get very slightly warmer. Which button is about that?

steps.answerWhy: On each bounce some energy warms the ball and floor or leaves as sound, so less is left to lift the ball.

steps.text: The energy transferred by heating and by sound ends up in the thermal stores of the ball, the floor and the air around them. Energy spread out like that is said to be dissipated.
Add the dissipated energy to what the ball still has, and the total is the same as at the start.
A system is the object, or group of objects, you are looking at. A system that no energy can get into or out of is called a closed system, and its total energy always stays the same.

steps.question: A ball bounces until it stops. Take the ball, the floor and the air around them as a closed system. Where is the energy the ball started with now?

options.text: In the thermal stores of the ball, floor and air
Still in the ball's gravitational potential store

steps.right: Yes. The total is the same as at the start; it is now spread through the thermal stores of the ball, the floor and the air.

wrong.other: Not quite. The energy is now in the thermal stores of the ball, the floor and the air; the total has not changed.
wrong.zero: Not quite: energy is never destroyed. The ball has stopped, but its energy is now in the thermal stores of the ball, floor and air.
wrong.gpe: Not quite: the ball is lying on the floor, so it is no longer raised up. Its energy is now in the thermal stores of the ball, floor and air.

idk.hint: The ball, the floor and the air all got very slightly warmer. Which button says where the energy is?

steps.answerWhy: The energy is now in the thermal stores of the ball, floor and air, and the total is the same as at the start.

steps.prompt: In one line: why does a bouncing ball bounce lower each time, and is any energy destroyed?
points: on each bounce some energy is dissipated to the surroundings (heating, sound)
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: on each bounce some energy is dissipated to the surroundings by heating and sound, but none is destroyed.

steps.text: In any transfer, the energy that goes where you want it is called useful energy. A lamp is meant to light a room, so the energy it sends out as light is useful.

Any energy that goes somewhere you did not want is called wasted energy. A lamp also warms the air around it, and that energy is wasted. Wasted energy is not lost: it is dissipated into the thermal store of the surroundings, where it is no use.

steps.question: A car engine burns fuel. Which of these is useful energy?

options.text: The energy that makes the car move
The energy that heats the exhaust
The energy carried away by the engine's noise

steps.right: Yes: the engine's job is to make the car move, so the energy in the car's kinetic store is useful. The energy that heats the engine and exhaust, and the noise, is wasted.

wrong.other: Not quite. The engine's job is to make the car move, so the useful energy is the energy in its kinetic store.
wrong.exhaust: Not quite: nobody wants a hot exhaust. That energy is wasted. The useful energy goes into the car's kinetic store.
wrong.noise: Not quite: the noise is wasted energy. The engine's job is to make the car move, so the useful energy goes into its kinetic store.

idk.hint: A car engine is there to make the car go. Which button is about that?

steps.answerWhy: The engine's job is to make the car move, so the useful energy is the energy in the car's kinetic store.

steps.text: Engineers try to waste less energy. One way is to cut friction: a force that tries to stop surfaces sliding over each other. Rub your hands together and they get warm; that warming comes from friction.
In a machine, friction between moving parts wastes energy by heating them. Putting oil between the parts lets them slide more easily. Using oil like this is called lubrication.

steps.question: A bicycle chain is squeaky and gets warm as you ride. After it is oiled, what changes?

options.text: Less energy is wasted heating the chain, because friction is smaller
The chain gets hotter, because oil burns
Nothing: oil only stops the squeak

steps.right: Yes: the oil reduces friction, so less energy is wasted heating the chain, and less is wasted as squeaks too.

wrong.other: Not quite. The oil reduces friction, so less energy is wasted heating the chain.
wrong.hotter: Not quite: the oil does not burn. It lets the parts slide more easily, so friction is smaller and less energy is wasted heating the chain.
wrong.nothing: Not quite: the squeak goes, but there is more to it. The oil reduces friction, so less energy is wasted heating the chain.

idk.hint: Oil makes surfaces slide more easily, so there is less friction. Which button says what that does to the heating?

steps.answerWhy: The oil reduces friction, so less energy is wasted heating the chain.

steps.prompt: In one line: what is useful energy, and what is wasted energy?
points: useful energy does the job you want
wasted energy goes somewhere you did not want
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: useful energy does the job you want, and wasted energy goes somewhere you did not want, usually warming the surroundings.

steps.text: Dissipation, the spreading out of energy into the surroundings, happens all the time.
Everything is made of tiny particles. Dissipated energy is shared among a huge number of them, so the surroundings warm by only a tiny amount, and the energy is very hard to collect and use again.
Dissipation happens wherever there is friction. A bike tyre skidding on a road gets hot, and a sliding box warms the floor a little.
Dissipation happens in wires too. A flow of electric charge through a wire is called a current. A current heats the wire it flows through, so some energy is dissipated.
And dissipation happens with sound. When sound hits a wall, the wall absorbs it, and the energy ends up in the thermal store of the wall.

steps.question: Which of these wastes energy because of friction?

options.text: A door hinge getting warm as it squeaks
A curtain soaking up the sound of a TV

steps.right: Yes: the parts of the hinge rub against each other as the door swings, and friction transfers energy to their thermal store.

wrong.other: Not quite: the door hinge. Its parts rub together, and friction warms them.
wrong.wire: Not quite: the charger warms because a current flows through it, not because of friction. The parts of the door hinge rub together.
wrong.sound: Not quite: the curtain absorbs sound; nothing rubs. The parts of the door hinge rub together, and friction warms them.

idk.hint: Friction happens when two surfaces rub. In which button are two parts rubbing together?

steps.answerWhy: The parts of the hinge rub against each other, and friction transfers energy to their thermal store.

steps.prompt: In one line: give one way energy gets dissipated, and say where it ends up.
points: friction, a current in a wire, or sound being absorbed
it ends up in a thermal store: of the surroundings, or of the wall
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: friction dissipates energy, and it ends up in the thermal store of the surroundings.

steps.text: Back to wasting less energy, this time in buildings. The main problem is warmth escaping on cold days.
Energy passes through a material from its hotter part to its colder part. This is called conduction. A metal spoon in hot tea gets a warm handle by conduction.

How easily energy is conducted through a material is called the thermal conductivity of the material. The higher the thermal conductivity, the faster energy passes through. Metals have a high thermal conductivity; air and foam have a low one.

steps.question: A pan handle is made of plastic, not metal. Why?

options.text: Plastic has a lower thermal conductivity
Plastic has a higher thermal conductivity
Plastic stops all energy getting through

steps.right: Yes: energy passes through plastic much more slowly than through metal, so the handle stays cool enough to hold.

wrong.other: Not quite. Plastic has a lower thermal conductivity, so energy passes through it slowly and the handle stays cooler.
wrong.higher: Not quite: the other way round. Plastic has a lower thermal conductivity than metal, so energy passes through it more slowly.
wrong.stops: Not quite: no material stops energy completely. Plastic has a low thermal conductivity, so it slows the energy down.

idk.hint: A handle should stay cool, so energy should pass through it slowly. Does that need a high or a low thermal conductivity?

steps.answerWhy: Plastic has a lower thermal conductivity than metal, so energy passes through it slowly and the handle stays cooler.

steps.text: Thermal insulation is any material or design that slows the transfer of energy to the surroundings. It uses materials with a low thermal conductivity, often with air trapped inside.
Homes use thermal insulation in several places. Fibre glass laid in the loft traps air, which slows energy escaping through the roof.
Double glazing is two panes of glass with a gap of air between them. Air has a low thermal conductivity, so the gap slows energy escaping through the window.

Many brick walls are two walls with a gap between them, called a cavity. Cavity wall insulation fills the gap with foam, which traps the air in tiny pockets so it cannot move about, slowing energy escaping even more.
The walls themselves matter too. Thicker walls, and walls made of a material with a lower thermal conductivity, both make a building cool down more slowly.

steps.question: Three houses are the same except for their walls. Which one cools down fastest on a cold night?

options.text: Thin walls of a material with a high thermal conductivity
Thick walls of a material with a low thermal conductivity
Thick walls of a material with a high thermal conductivity

steps.right: Yes: thin walls and a high thermal conductivity both let energy out faster.

wrong.other: Not quite: the house with thin walls of a high thermal conductivity material. Both let energy out faster.
wrong.thicklow: Not quite: thick walls of a low thermal conductivity material keep a house warm longest. The fastest to cool has thin walls with a high thermal conductivity.
wrong.thickhigh: Not quite: thick walls slow the energy down. The fastest to cool has thin walls and a high thermal conductivity.

idk.hint: Thicker walls slow cooling. A lower thermal conductivity slows cooling. Which house has neither?

steps.answerWhy: Thin walls and a high thermal conductivity both let energy out faster, so that house cools fastest.

steps.text: You can compare insulating materials in a lab. Put the same amount of hot water in identical cans, wrap each can in a different material, and measure how far the temperature falls in, say, ten minutes.
The thing you change on purpose is called the independent variable. In this test it is the material.
The thing you measure is called the dependent variable. Here it is the fall in temperature.
Everything else must stay the same: the volume of water, its starting temperature, the time, and the thickness of each material. These are called the control variables.

steps.question: In this test, what is the dependent variable?
steps.right: Yes: it is what you measure.

wrong.other: Not quite: the fall in temperature, which is what you measure.
wrong.indep: Not quite: the material is what you change on purpose, the independent variable. What you measure, the fall in temperature, is the dependent variable.
wrong.control: Not quite: the volume of water is kept the same, so it is a control variable. What you measure, the fall in temperature, is the dependent variable.

idk.hint: The dependent variable is the thing you measure. What do you measure with the thermometer?

steps.answerWhy: The dependent variable is what you measure: the fall in temperature.

steps.question: In the test, which material is the best insulator?

options.text: The one whose water temperature falls the least
The one whose water temperature falls the most

steps.right: Yes: the best insulator lets the least energy out, so its water cools the least.

wrong.other: Not quite. The best insulator lets the least energy out, so its water temperature falls the least.
wrong.most: Not quite: the other way round. The best insulator lets the least energy out, so its water cools the least.
wrong.thin: Not quite: all the materials are the same thickness in a fair test. The best insulator is the one whose water cools the least.

idk.hint: A good insulator keeps energy in. Would that water cool a lot or a little?

steps.answerWhy: The best insulator lets the least energy out, so its water temperature falls the least.

steps.text: The same kind of test can look at other factors. Keep the material the same and change its thickness, or the number of layers. Then the thickness, or the number of layers, is the independent variable.

One more way to waste less energy, this time for moving things. Air resistance is the push of the air on anything moving through it. A moving car wastes energy from its kinetic store pushing the air out of the way.
Shaping something so air flows smoothly round it is called streamlining, like a sports car or a cyclist's helmet. It reduces air resistance, so less energy is wasted.

steps.question: A delivery van has a flat, square front. Engineers give it a smooth, rounded front. Why does that waste less energy?

options.text: Less air resistance, so less energy wasted pushing the air
Less friction between the tyres and road

steps.right: Yes: the rounded shape is streamlined, so the air pushes back less and less energy is wasted.

wrong.other: Not quite. The rounded front is streamlined, so there is less air resistance and less energy is wasted.
wrong.friction: Not quite: the shape of the front does not change the tyres. It reduces air resistance, so less energy is wasted pushing the air.
wrong.more: Not quite: no engine makes energy. The streamlined shape reduces air resistance, so less energy is wasted pushing the air.

idk.hint: The front of the van pushes through the air. What does a smooth, rounded shape reduce?

steps.answerWhy: The rounded front is streamlined, so air resistance is smaller and less energy is wasted.

steps.prompt: In one line: name the three ways in this lesson to reduce wasted energy.
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: lubrication to reduce friction, thermal insulation to slow energy escaping, and streamlining to reduce air resistance.

steps.text: Now for a short quiz: six questions across the lesson. Take your time.

steps.question: Quiz, question 1 of 6: which is true about energy?

options.text: It cannot be created or destroyed
It is used up when things stop

steps.right: Yes: that is the law of conservation of energy.

wrong.other: Not quite. Energy cannot be created or destroyed: that is the law of conservation of energy.
wrong.w1: Not quite: energy is not used up when things stop. It is dissipated into the surroundings; the total stays the same.
wrong.w2: Not quite: no machine makes new energy. Machines only transfer energy from one store to another.

steps.answerWhy: Energy cannot be created or destroyed: the law of conservation of energy.

steps.question: Quiz, question 2 of 6: what does lubrication reduce?
steps.right: Yes: oil reduces friction between moving parts.

wrong.other: Not quite: friction. Oil between moving parts reduces friction.
wrong.w1: Not quite: friction. Air resistance is reduced by streamlining, not oil.
wrong.w2: Not quite: friction. Thermal conductivity belongs to a material; oil cannot change it. Oil reduces friction between moving parts.

steps.answerWhy: Lubrication reduces friction between moving parts.

steps.question: Quiz, question 3 of 6: a material with a high thermal conductivity…
steps.right: Yes: the higher the thermal conductivity, the faster energy passes through.

wrong.other: Not quite: a high thermal conductivity means energy passes through quickly.
wrong.w1: Not quite: a good insulator has a low thermal conductivity. A high one means energy passes through quickly.
wrong.w2: Not quite: nothing stops energy completely. A high thermal conductivity means energy passes through quickly.

steps.answerWhy: The higher the thermal conductivity, the faster energy passes through.

steps.question: Quiz, question 4 of 6: why do thicker walls keep a house warm for longer?

options.text: Energy passes through them more slowly

steps.right: Yes: thicker walls slow the energy escaping.

wrong.other: Not quite: thicker walls slow the energy escaping; they do not stop it or make energy.

steps.answerWhy: Thicker walls make energy pass through more slowly.

steps.question: Quiz, question 5 of 6: in the insulation test, which is a control variable?
steps.right: Yes: it is kept the same so the test is fair.

wrong.other: Not quite: the volume of hot water is kept the same, so it is a control variable. The material is changed, and the fall in temperature is measured.

steps.answerWhy: The volume of hot water is kept the same, so it is a control variable.

steps.question: Quiz, question 6 of 6: which reduces the air resistance on a car?
steps.right: Yes: a streamlined shape lets the air flow round it smoothly.

wrong.other: Not quite: streamlining, shaping the car so air flows round it smoothly.
wrong.w1: Not quite: lubrication reduces friction between moving parts. Streamlining, a smooth shape, reduces air resistance.
wrong.w2: Not quite: double glazing slows energy escaping through windows. Streamlining, a smooth shape, reduces air resistance.

steps.text: That's the end of the quiz: you got {right} out of {n}.

end.text: The lesson is finished. Tap a button to go on.
